context.title: Young People Abandoning Email
body: A youth-technology column reports that teenagers now favour instant messages, social-media chats and short voice notes for everyday conversation. Email remains important for school applications, receipts and contact with organisations, but its subject lines, greetings and formal tone can feel unfamiliar to inexperienced writers.

Supporters of email value its searchable record, ability to attach documents and usefulness across different platforms. Others say that crowded inboxes and slow replies make it unsuitable for urgent or friendly exchanges.

The writer asks whether email is disappearing or simply becoming a more specialised form of communication. A school careers adviser recently returned three applications because their messages had no subject line, no greeting and unexplained attachments. She now runs a short email clinic where students compare a chat message with a request to an employer. Her advice is simple: choose the channel to match the reader, and proofread formal messages before pressing send. The clinic also demonstrates when a reply-all message creates unnecessary confusion.

context.title: Airport Ambassadors
body: Hong Kong International Airport is inviting young adults to serve as Airport Ambassadors at busy passenger areas. Ambassadors greet travellers, answer questions, give directions, assist people in difficulty and help communicate safety messages. Training is provided before they begin work.

The role offers customer-service experience and a close look at aviation and tourism. However, ambassadors must stand for long periods, remain calm with tired passengers and communicate across language and cultural differences.

Applicants need to decide whether this demanding public-facing role is a useful opportunity for young people. On a crowded evening shift, one ambassador might guide a family to a transfer desk while another explains a delay to an anxious traveller. The work suits people who notice confusion quickly and give clear answers without sounding impatient. A young recruit may find the airport tiring at first, yet each encounter offers practice in languages, judgement and courtesy. Rotating duties would help newcomers build confidence before facing the busiest arrival periods.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style mock context for 2014 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.3; not reproduced from the examination paper.
context.title: Helicopter Parenting
body: A family magazine describes “helicopter parents” as adults who closely supervise almost every part of a child’s life. They may check homework repeatedly, select activities, contact teachers about small problems and try to prevent their children from making mistakes.

Such attention can provide safety and support, especially when children are young. Yet constant control may weaken confidence, independence and problem-solving skills, while also causing arguments at home.

The article asks how parents can remain caring and involved without preventing teenagers from learning through experience. One teenager in the article describes a parent who rewrote a school presentation without being asked; another appreciates being collected late at night but wants to choose her own friends. Family counsellors suggest agreeing in advance which decisions belong to the child. Advice is most useful when it helps a young person act, rather than replacing the action altogether. Regular family meetings can revisit those boundaries as trust and maturity develop.

context.title: Food Photography
body: A lifestyle website notes that photographing meals has become a normal part of eating out for many young people. Colourful dishes can be shared instantly with friends, used to record special occasions or collected as recommendations for other diners.

Restaurant owners may benefit from free publicity, and careful food photography can be creative. On the other hand, repeated photo-taking can delay a meal, disturb companions and encourage people to judge food mainly by appearance.

A successful food blog therefore needs attractive images, honest comments, clear organisation and respect for other diners. For the proposed student blog, each post could pair one carefully framed image with the dish name, price, location and a brief comment on taste. Bloggers should ask before photographing another person’s plate and avoid blocking restaurant aisles. Readers are more likely to trust a page that includes ordinary meals and disappointments, not only perfectly arranged desserts. A simple rating guide would make separate reviews easier to compare.

context.title: Street Culture in Hong Kong
body: Street dance, skateboarding, graffiti art and outdoor performance are becoming more visible in Hong Kong. Young participants say these activities provide an affordable space for creativity, friendship and self-expression, especially when indoor venues are limited.

Some residents associate street groups with noise, damage or unsafe behaviour. Participants respond that most performers respect public space and that clear rules and suitable venues would reduce conflict.

Community events, demonstrations and cooperation with local organisations may help the public judge street culture by its actual behaviour rather than by stereotypes. A district youth centre has offered its outdoor wall for supervised mural sessions and marked a smooth corner for weekend skating. Residents can watch demonstrations, speak to performers and report genuine nuisance through one contact person. The arrangement does not excuse damage or dangerous tricks; it gives responsible participants a place to show that street activity can be skilled and organised. Evening closing times would also answer neighbours’ concerns about noise.

context.source_line: Original HKEAA-style mock context for 2014 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.3; not reproduced from the examination paper.
context.title: Happiness in Hong Kong and Switzerland
body: An international report places Switzerland among the world’s happiest societies while Hong Kong appears much lower in the table. The comparison highlights health care, education, innovation and infrastructure. Both places are prosperous and highly connected, but residents may experience public services, housing, work pressure and community life differently.

Rankings can reveal broad patterns, yet a single number cannot capture every person’s situation or every cultural view of happiness. Economic success may improve security without automatically creating leisure, trust or belonging.

Readers are invited to consider which Swiss strengths could transfer to Hong Kong and which local conditions require different solutions. Hong Kong already performs strongly in transport and digital connections, but long working hours and expensive housing affect daily satisfaction. A Swiss policy cannot simply be copied into a denser city with different public finances. Local experiments might begin with accessible health support, less pressured school routines and neighbourhood spaces where residents can meet without paying to enter.

context.title: Urban Dictionary
body: Online dictionaries allow users to submit new slang, abbreviations and expressions before they appear in traditional reference books. These entries can show how language changes through music, social media and youth culture, but definitions are written by volunteers and may be inaccurate, offensive or short-lived.

A student dictionary could collect authentic examples from conversations, songs and online posts while checking meaning with several speakers. Editors would also need rules on relevance, clarity and respectful language.

Images, example sentences and short notes about origin could make the final dictionary informative without suggesting that every popular expression belongs in formal English. Editors at one school propose accepting a word only after finding it in three independent examples and confirming its meaning with several students. Each entry would show pronunciation, context and a warning if the expression is rude or unsuitable for formal work. Monthly online updates would handle fast-changing slang, while a printed selection would preserve the most useful terms.

context.title: Finland's Education System
body: An education feature describes Finland’s later school starting age, limited standardised testing, mixed-ability classes and strong teacher training. The system is often praised for equality and professional trust. Hong Kong, by contrast, offers a broad school network, strong academic expectations and clear public examination routes.

Practices that succeed in one country depend on culture, resources, population and university admission systems. Removing examinations or homework without changing other structures may not produce the same results.

Rather than declaring one system superior, students should identify useful principles and decide which changes would be realistic and fair in Hong Kong. A Hong Kong principal visiting Helsinki is impressed by calm classrooms and the time teachers spend planning together. She also notes that local schools serve larger populations and prepare pupils for a competitive public examination. Her trial plan keeps regular assessment but replaces one homework exercise each week with guided reading, teacher feedback and mixed-ability problem solving.

context.title: Ferris Wheel on the Central Waterfront
body: A proposal suggests building a large Ferris wheel on the Central waterfront, with air-conditioned cabins and harbour views. Supporters expect a recognisable attraction that could bring visitors and business to the area. Tickets, operating hours and nearby events could make the site lively during the day and at night.
Critics question whether Hong Kong should copy attractions in other cities and whether valuable public land could serve residents better as open space, cultural facilities or a waterfront park.

The decision depends on cost, originality, public access and the long-term value of the whole waterfront rather than on visitor numbers alone. Under one design, the wheel would occupy the site for a limited period and pay rent towards waterfront maintenance. A competing plan proposes lawns, a small performance stage, shaded seating and space for weekend markets. Public access between attractions and the harbour edge remains crucial: a landmark loses much of its value if queues, ticket barriers and shops dominate the promenade.

context.title: Communicating with Parents through Social Media
body: A survey finds that many parents monitor teenagers’ social-media use, sometimes by following them directly and sometimes by creating another account. Parents say they worry about strangers, bullying, harmful posts and the amount of personal information shared online. Teenagers may understand these risks but still want a private space to talk with friends.

Monitoring can reveal a serious problem early, yet secret checking may damage trust and encourage young people to hide more. Clear family rules and open conversations may be more effective than demanding passwords.

Families need to balance safety, privacy and respect while recognising that the right level of supervision changes as children grow older. A useful family agreement might specify which platforms a teenager may use, what information must stay private and when an adult should intervene. Parents would promise not to post embarrassing childhood photographs or comment on every conversation. Teenagers, in return, would report threats and unknown contacts. Such rules make online safety a shared responsibility rather than a secret investigation.

context.title: Couponing
body: Discount coupons now appear in newspapers, mobile applications, shop memberships and social-media promotions. Students may use them for meals, drinks, entertainment or online shopping. A good offer can reduce the cost of something they already planned to buy.

Couponing can become time-consuming, and limited-time deals may encourage unnecessary purchases. Conditions such as minimum spending, restricted dates and data collection can make a discount less valuable than it first appears.

Consumer groups recommend keeping a list, calculating the full bill and deleting unused offers before they expire. A coupon works best as a reduction on a planned purchase, not as a reason to create one.

body: A health column lists everyday mistakes such as skipping breakfast, carrying heavy bags, sleeping too little, exercising incorrectly and trusting unverified advice. Anonymous question cards would let students raise sensitive concerns, while printed sources would separate medical guidance from online rumours. Follow-up cards could invite pupils to track one small change for seven days.

context.title: Compulsory Courtesy Classes in Secondary Schools
body: A proposal calls for secondary schools to teach courtesy through formal lessons rather than relying only on family guidance and school rules. Possible topics include respectful conversation, behaviour on public transport, online manners, conflict resolution and consideration for people with different needs.

Supporters say shared lessons could improve the school climate. Critics argue that good manners are learned through daily examples and that compulsory classes may become artificial or take time from other subjects.

Junior students practise simple public behaviour, while older classes examine workplace and online situations. Teachers would judge the programme by fewer repeated conflicts and more considerate routines, not by a manners test.

context.title: The Social Impact of Advertising
body: Advertising pays for media, informs consumers about products and can introduce useful services or public campaigns. Creative advertisements may entertain audiences and help small companies reach customers. Competition can also encourage businesses to explain price, quality and new features.

At the same time, repeated messages may create unrealistic expectations, encourage wasteful consumption or influence children who cannot easily judge commercial claims. Products linked to health, addiction or financial risk raise particular concerns.

Clear labelling and limits on audience targeting may protect consumers while allowing legitimate businesses to speak, whereas dangerous or deliberately deceptive products justify stronger restrictions.

body: Some restaurants attract attention by offering unusually large portions for sharing, challenges or social-media photos. A super-sized item can create excitement and may appear good value when several friends order together. It can also make a school food stall memorable.

Customers could choose a normal or challenge size, and untouched ingredients could be prepared only when ordered. A visible portion guide and reusable sharing trays would preserve the fun photograph while controlling waste, cost and pressure to overeat.

context.title: Technology Addiction
body: A youth-health report warns that some teenagers spend many hours moving between computers, phones, games and social-media platforms. Technology supports study, entertainment and friendships, so heavy use alone does not prove addiction. Concern grows when use regularly interrupts sleep, schoolwork, exercise or face-to-face relationships.
Notifications, rewards in games and fear of missing out can make stopping difficult. Families may impose limits, but sudden bans can create conflict or ignore the reasons a young person stays online.

Tracking habits, turning off unnecessary alerts and planning offline activities may help users regain control while keeping the benefits of technology. One class tries a seven-day log and discovers that most late-night screen time begins with “just one” notification. Students move chargers outside bedrooms, set game stopping points and arrange a phone-free lunch with friends. Anyone whose use causes serious distress should speak to a counsellor rather than rely on willpower alone. The target is controlled use, not life without screens.

context.title: Study Time in Hong Kong
body: A proposal suggests setting aside 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. as daily “Study Time” for schoolchildren, with families expected to protect the period from distractions. Supporters believe a shared routine could improve concentration and encourage parents to create quiet conditions at home.

Opponents question enforcement and fairness. Students have different learning needs, tutoring schedules, homes and responsibilities, while fixed evening study may reduce sleep, exercise and family time.

A two-week neighbourhood trial offers quiet rooms in libraries and schools during the proposed hours but does not punish families who follow another routine. Participants record concentration, sleep and unfinished work. If younger pupils benefit while older students feel constrained, the scheme could remain an optional support service instead of becoming a territory-wide rule backed by penalties. Weekend athletes and evening carers must also be included in the evaluation.

context.title: Discipline and Children in Hong Kong
body: A parenting feature compares child-centred decision-making with stricter family rules. Allowing children to express preferences can build confidence and responsibility, but adults still need to set boundaries on safety, money, study and respectful behaviour.

Consistent discipline may teach self-control and consequences. Harsh, unpredictable or unexplained punishment can instead create fear, secrecy and resentment, especially when children have no chance to explain themselves.

The central issue is not whether children should have a voice, but how families can combine age-appropriate freedom with clear and fair limits. In one family, children choose the weekend activity but adults decide the spending limit and return time. Broken rules lead to related consequences, such as losing use of an item that was misused, followed by a calm explanation. The arrangement gives children meaningful choices without making them responsible for adult matters. Discipline becomes teaching, not a contest over control. Parents must follow the agreed rules consistently if they expect children to respect them.

context.title: Dance and Teenagers in Hong Kong
body: School dance groups include styles ranging from traditional and social dance to hip-hop and contemporary performance. Teenagers may join because of popular music, friends, exercise or the chance to perform. Rehearsal can develop fitness, rhythm, cooperation, confidence and persistence.

Some students worry about embarrassment, cost or lack of experience, while demanding rehearsals may conflict with study. Beginner sessions and different performance roles can make the group more welcoming.

Demonstrations, lunchtime workshops and student-created videos could attract interest if the campaign presents dance as both an art and an inclusive activity. The group plans an open rehearsal where visitors learn one short routine in ordinary sports clothes. A lunchtime showcase would combine a traditional piece, street dance and student choreography, followed by information on beginner practices. Filming should require performers’ consent. Showing the preparation behind a polished performance may persuade hesitant students that dance is learned step by step, not an inborn gift.

context.title: Choosing Magazines for the School Library
body: The school library has enough money for only one of several proposed magazine subscriptions aimed at teenagers. The choices vary in price, subject matter, reading level, design and frequency. A popular entertainment magazine may attract more readers, while a news or science title may support schoolwork.
Print issues are easy to browse but require storage and can become dated. Online editions may provide searchable archives, yet access limits and screen reading can reduce their usefulness.

The library should consider student demand, reliability, educational value and whether one subscription can serve a broad range of readers. Librarians could display sample issues for a fortnight and record which sections pupils actually read. The final choice might include a digital archive if its licence allows many users, or a print title that circulates well between classes. Future subscriptions should fill gaps in science, current affairs, arts and practical hobbies rather than buying several magazines that repeat celebrity news.
